title: Anıtkabir, done properly
tagline: The republic's founder under a limestone colonnade on a hill over the city — the one place in Ankara that every Turk visits, and the reason to walk slowly.
when: a weekday morning — or 10 November at 09:05, once, for the silence
why: Anıtkabir is Atatürk's mausoleum, built between 1944 and 1953 on Rasattepe, a hill west of Kızılay that looks over the whole city. You approach along the Aslanlı Yol, a 260-metre road lined with Hittite-style stone lions, into a vast ceremonial square, and up the steps to the hall of honour where the tomb sits under a single 40-tonne sarcophagus. Beneath it all is the Atatürk and War of Independence Museum: Atatürk's cars, library and clothes, and panoramic dioramas of the battles. What makes the place more than a monument is how it is used — school groups, soldiers, couples, grandmothers, all of Turkey passing through in near-silence. On 10 November at 09:05, the minute of his death, the square is full and the city stops. Entry is free and it is open every day of the year.
take: Go once alone and once with visitors. Alone, go early on a weekday, walk the lion road slowly (the stones are laid with gaps rather than flush, and the story goes that this was deliberate, so you walk with your eyes down), then spend real time in the museum below — the dioramas explain why this country exists in a way nothing else in Ankara does. Watch a changing of the guard at the top of the hour. With a group, it is our easiest first Smileys outing: free, central, and everyone has something to say afterwards. There is an airport-style security check at the gate, so travel light; dress as you would for a serious place, and be quiet in the hall. Hours shift with the seasons — roughly nine to five, longer on national days — ⚠ VERIFY the current closing time on anitkabir.tsk.tr before you promise a late-afternoon visit.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The Aslanlı Yol — walk it, don't rush it; the lions are Hittite by design, a deliberate claim on Anatolia's whole past.
The hall of honour — the sarcophagus and the ceiling mosaics; keep your voice down.
The museum under the mausoleum — the war dioramas and Atatürk's library are the reason to give it two hours.
The changing of the guard on the hour in the square.
Look back from the top step: the city, the citadel on its rock, and on a clear winter day snow on Elmadağ.

title: The citadel, the copper lanes and the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
tagline: Hittites in a fifteenth-century bedesten, coppersmiths on the hill below, and the whole city from a Byzantine wall — Ankara's oldest corner in one afternoon.
when: afternoon — museum first, then the walls for sunset
why: Long before it was a capital, Ankara was this rock. The citadel walls are Byzantine on Roman foundations, and inside them a village of timber houses still lives its own life — cats, laundry, a mosque older than the republic. On the southeast slope below, two Ottoman market buildings, the Mahmut Paşa bedesteni and the Kurşunlu Han, hold the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations: the richest Hittite collection anywhere, the Çatalhöyük finds, Phrygian furniture from Gordion, ten thousand years of Anatolia in two rooms. Across the lane, Çengelhan (1520s) is the Rahmi M. Koç industrial museum. Between the gate and Ulus run the old trade lanes — Atpazarı, Çıkrıkçılar Yokuşu and the Bakırcılar coppersmiths' market — where you can still hear hammers on metal. The municipality's inner-castle restoration finished its main phases in 2025, so the lanes are in the best shape they have been in decades.
take: Start with the museum and give it two hours — it is small enough not to exhaust you and good enough to change how you see every field you drive past afterwards. Then climb through the inner castle to the eastern tower and stay for the light: Ankara is a bowl of hills and this is the rim. Come down the copper lanes rather than the road, and stop for tea at the foot. The museum keeps standard state-museum hours (the ticket office closes at 16:45 in winter) and opens only from 13:00 on the first day of a religious bayram; Çengelhan closes on Mondays. Both are ticketed; the castle and the lanes are free. It's a walk we do with every newcomer, and one we repeat every time a friend visits.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The Hittite hall — the reliefs from Alacahöyük and Carchemish, and the Kültepe tablets.
The Çatalhöyük room — the wall painting that may be the world's oldest map.
Çengelhan Rahmi M. Koç Museum — old cars, radios and a working pharmacy; a good rainy-day pairing.
The Bakırcılar (coppersmiths) lane and Çıkrıkçılar Yokuşu — buy a cezve from the man who made it.
Sunset from the inner-castle walls; the safest way up is via the main gate and the marked steps.

title: Ulus: the first parliament, the Roman baths and Hacı Bayram
tagline: Where the republic was declared, where Augustus carved his own obituary, and where Ankara still comes to pray — all within ten minutes' walk.
when: a weekday morning; Fridays are crowded at the mosque
why: Ulus is the old centre — the town Atatürk reached by car from Sivas on 27 December 1919, and the square where the republic was run for its first decade. On it stand the First Grand National Assembly building, where parliament met from 1920 to 1924 and which is now the Kurtuluş Savaşı (War of Independence) Museum, and the Second Assembly a few doors down, now the Cumhuriyet Museum. Ten minutes north on Çankırı Caddesi are the Roman baths of Ancyra, built under Caracalla in the third century and laid out as an open-air museum of steles and inscriptions. Uphill is Hacı Bayram Veli's fifteenth-century mosque and tomb — the city's spiritual centre — built hard against the Temple of Augustus, whose walls carry the emperor's own account of his reign, the Res Gestae, in the best-preserved copy anywhere. Nowhere else in Turkey puts Rome, the Sufis and the republic on one hillside.
take: Do it as a loop from Ulus square: the first parliament first (it is small, and standing in the room where the country was invented is the point), then the baths, then up to Hacı Bayram. The mosque is very much in use — go between prayers, cover up, and expect pilgrims, wedding parties and pigeons. The Augustus temple is under permanent steel bracing and has been for years; you see it through a fence, which is still worth it — ⚠ VERIFY whether the site itself is open before promising a group the inscriptions up close. The state museums here take Müze Kart, which pays for itself in a week in this city. Finish with a simit and tea in the square: Ulus is scruffier than Çankaya and we like it more for that.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Kurtuluş Savaşı Museum (I. TBMM) on Ulus square — the assembly hall with the original desks.
Cumhuriyet Museum (II. TBMM) a few doors along Cumhuriyet Caddesi.
Roman Baths open-air museum on Çankırı Caddesi — quieter than it has any right to be.
Hacı Bayram mosque and tomb, and the Temple of Augustus beside it.
Ulus is the metro's Ulus stop; the whole loop is flat except the last climb to the mosque.

title: An evening in Hamamönü
tagline: A restored Ottoman quarter below the citadel — konaks turned into tea gardens, a bath from 1440, and the house where the national anthem was written.
when: late afternoon into evening; Ramadan nights are the busiest and the best
why: Hamamönü is the neighbourhood that fell down the hill from the citadel and was, until fifteen years ago, close to derelict. Altındağ municipality restored it street by street from 2009, and what came back is a small grid of two-storey timber houses in ochre, white and blue, cobbles, courtyards, and the hamam it is named after — the Karacabey hamamı of 1440, still a working bath, and the Taceddin dergâh where Mehmet Akif Ersoy wrote the İstiklal Marşı in 1921. Today the konaks are tea gardens, craft workshops, small art houses and restaurants doing home cooking; there is an open-air stage for concerts, and during Ramadan the whole quarter turns into an evening fair after iftar. It is touristy in a very local way — the visitors are Ankara families, not tour buses.
take: Come at the end of a citadel afternoon: down through the lanes, into Hamamönü as the lamps come on, and take a table in a konak courtyard for a çay and a plate of gözleme. Look into the Taceddin house (free, tiny, moving if you know the anthem) and the craft houses, where you can usually watch someone at work. It is our standard 'first evening with a new group' spot — safe, cheap, easy to find, and full of people who will talk to you. Be honest about the limits: it's small, it is polished rather than raw, and outside Ramadan and weekends it can be quiet by nine. Pair it with Sakarya afterwards if the night wants to keep going.

title: Fish, beer and students on Sakarya Caddesi
tagline: Kızılay's pedestrian strip — fried anchovies and a cold Efes on a plastic stool, kokoreç at midnight, and the loudest, youngest crowd in the capital.
when: a term-time Thursday or Friday from 7pm; summer evenings are quieter
why: Kızılay is Ankara's crossroads — the metro lines meet under it, the civil servants pour out of it at five, and the students of Hacettepe, Ankara University and Gazi treat it as their living room. Sakarya Caddesi and the lanes around it (Selanik, Bayındır, Tuna) are the pedestrian core: a strip of fish restaurants and beer halls, midye and kokoreç stands, cheap grill houses and pubs stacked two floors deep, where the standard order is a plate of hamsi or a fried fish sandwich, a beer, and a table you'll end up sharing. It is the most democratic square kilometre in a city with a lot of hierarchy in it, and the noise is the point.
take: This is where we send anyone who says Ankara is boring. Go with two or three people, not ten; sit outside if the weather allows; order fish and beer and let the evening happen. The kokoreç at the top of the street is the correct 1am. Don't expect polish or quiet — this is student Ankara at full volume, with the Güvenpark buses grumbling past. Kızılay is safe and very well lit, but pickpockets like crowds anywhere, so keep the phone in the front pocket. Term time matters: in August half the tables are empty. Good news for newcomers under thirty-five, and honestly for everyone else too.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Start on Sakarya itself for fish and beer, then drift into Selanik and Bayındır for pubs.
Midye dolma from a cart is the between-drinks snack; kokoreç is the end of the night.
Güvenpark and Kızılay square are your landmarks — every metro and Ankaray line meets here.
Weeknights are locals; weekends bring the suburbs in.

title: Tunalı Hilmi, Kuğulu Park and the bars of Bestekar
tagline: The capital's polite side — a shopping avenue, swans in a park, and a side street that turns into Ankara's bar strip after dark.
when: late afternoon walk, then from 9pm on Bestekar
why: Kavaklıdere is embassy Ankara: tree-lined, tidy, expensive by local standards, and the part of the city that feels most like a European capital. Tunalı Hilmi Caddesi is its spine — a mile of shops, cafés and pastry houses that everyone just calls 'Tunalı' — and Kuğulu Park at the bottom is the small, beloved park with a pond and the swans that, the story goes, arrived as a gift from Vienna. Uphill toward Ayrancı the streets become residential and quiet. One block off Tunalı, Bestekar Sokak is where the district drinks: a run of bars, pubs and small music venues that fills every night of the week with diplomats' kids, university lecturers, journalists and the young professionals who make up most of the city. It is where most of our Ankara members already go.
take: Walk Tunalı from Kuğulu up to Kavaklıdere in the last hour of daylight — it is the best people-watching in the city and the easiest way to feel how many nationalities live here. Then pick a bar on Bestekar with tables outside and stay; the crowd is talkative, English is common, and in a small city you'll see the same faces within a month, which is exactly how community forms. Prices are above Kızılay and below Istanbul. Thursday is the local big night. If you want to meet Ankara's international crowd on your first week, this is the street.

title: Ankara's two dinner streets: Filistin Caddesi and 7. Cadde
tagline: One for a proper night out in the embassy quarter, one for cheap plates and cafés with the Bahçelievler students — learn both and you've learned how the city eats.
when: dinner from 8pm; 7. Cadde any time from breakfast
why: Ankara doesn't have a single restaurant district; it has streets. Filistin Caddesi in Gaziosmanpaşa — GOP, the neighbourhood above Kavaklıdere where the embassies and the ambassadors' residences are — is the grown-up one: a long avenue of restaurants doing Anatolian, Italian, Levantine and Turkish grill at mid-range prices, with terraces and a crowd that dresses for dinner. Across the city in Bahçelievler, 7. Cadde (formally Aşkabat Caddesi) is the opposite: a traffic-lined but pavement-led strip of cafés, cheap grill and pide houses, dessert shops and bars, kept alive by the students from nearby campuses and the families who have lived in Bahçelievler since it was a garden suburb in the 1930s. It runs from breakfast to past midnight and costs a fraction of GOP.
take: Use them differently. Filistin is where we book a table for a Smileys dinner of six or eight — quiet enough to talk, good enough to impress a visitor, and a ten-minute taxi from Kavaklıdere. 7. Cadde is the everyday one: meet for a çay, stay for a plate of something, move on to a bar, spend little. Both are honest about what they are, which is why we like them more than the malls. Try to keep to independent places rather than chains on either street; the city has plenty of the latter already. And a caution about Filistin: Ankara's dining scene turns over fast, so ask a local what's good this year rather than trusting a two-year-old list.

title: Eymir Lake: the loop, the bikes and the METU forest
tagline: A reed-fringed lake inside a university's own forest, free on foot, with a loop track that Ankara runs, cycles and walks its dogs around every weekend.
when: weekday afternoon; weekend mornings before ten
why: Middle East Technical University owns a forest — planted from bare steppe from the 1960s onwards, and now the biggest green mass in the city — and Eymir Lake, twenty minutes south of the centre, is its lake. METU runs it as a campus: a loop track of about eight kilometres around the water, a bike-hire shed at the gate, rowing sheds, tea houses and a few restaurants on the shore, reed beds full of birds, and no swimming, no camping, no drones. Entry on foot or by bicycle is free and open to everyone; only cars need a METU card, so most of Ankara parks outside and walks in. In a dry, treeless city, it is where people go to breathe, and on a Sunday morning it is half the population under thirty-five.
take: Rent a bike at the gate and do the loop once at your own pace, then a second time faster; or walk it with a group and stop at the far end for tea, which is our standard Smileys Saturday morning. Go on a weekday if you can — weekends are lovely but busy. Bring water and a layer; the wind off the steppe is real even in May. Practicalities: the gate closes to new visitors at 22:00 and everyone leaves by 23:30, and a car will not get past the barrier without a METU card, so plan on taxi or bus to the gate. The main METU campus in Çankaya is a different matter — visitors are admitted at the gate only with a METU host — so if you want the forest walks up there, make a METU friend first. ⚠ VERIFY the current visitor rule at the main campus gates; it has tightened and loosened several times.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Get to the Eymir gate by taxi or the Gölbaşı-road buses; walk or cycle in — cars need a METU card.
Bike hire is at the entrance; the loop is flat and roughly eight kilometres.
Tea and a simple lunch at the lakeside places; no swimming, no camping, no drones.
Last entry 22:00; everyone out by 23:30.
Combine with Mogan Lake in Gölbaşı, ten minutes further south, for a full day.

title: Mogan Lake and Gölbaşı
tagline: Ankara's other lake — a long lakeside park, kites, breakfast places and birds — and an honest word about the drought.
when: a spring or autumn weekend; summer evenings for the breeze
why: Twenty kilometres south of the city, Mogan is the bigger and shallower sibling of Eymir — six square kilometres of lake with reed beds, a protected wetland since 1990, and a municipal park (Mogan Park) along the northern shore with lawns, cycle paths, playgrounds and tea gardens. Gölbaşı, the town around it, is where central Ankara goes for a lakeside breakfast on Sunday and where families rent pedal boats and fly kites. It is one of the few places in the region that feels like water and open horizon. That comes with a caveat we won't hide: in the drought summer of 2025 the water pulled back from the shore, dead fish and mud were exposed and the smell and the flies made the front unwalkable in August. Turkey's wet 2026 winter refilled much of the country's water, but the lake's condition changes year to year.
take: Go for the park and the breakfast, and take the lake as you find it. In spring, when the storks and herons are back and the shore is green, it is a genuinely lovely half-day; in summer, go in the evening for the wind. Rent a pedal boat if the water is up. Combine with Eymir for a two-lake day by bike or taxi. Before you plan a Smileys outing here, ⚠ VERIFY the lake's current state — a quick look at recent local news or a member in Gölbaşı will tell you whether it's a picnic or a mudflat this month. We would rather tell you that than have you drive out to a smell.

title: Beypazarı: Ottoman houses, carrots and güveç
tagline: A hill town of three thousand timber houses ninety minutes west — meat and vegetables baked in clay, eighty-layer baklava, and a carrot on every corner.
when: a weekday if you can; the festival weekend at the end of September if you like a crowd
why: Beypazarı is the day trip every Ankara family has made: about a hundred kilometres north-west on the D140 Ayaş road, a town of steep lanes, and more than three thousand registered Ottoman houses in white plaster and dark timber, with bay windows leaning over the street. It was a stop on the Silk Road and a wealthy market town, and it has spent the last twenty-five years restoring itself and learning to feed visitors. The food is the point: güveç (lamb or beef baked with vegetables in an earthenware pot), yaprak sarma, tarhana soup, the 80-katlı baklava, the dry Beypazarı kurusu biscuits that go home in everyone's bag, and the town's own mineral water. And carrots — Beypazarı grows a large share of Turkey's, so there are carrot juices, carrot lokum and a carrot statue in the square. The international festival, running since 1994, is held over a long weekend in late September.
take: Take a shared car or the intercity bus from AŞTİ and give it the whole day. Walk the old quarter first, before lunch, climbing to the Hıdırlık viewpoint for the roof-tiles-and-hills panorama; then sit down for güveç, which takes time and should. Buy kurusu and mineral water for home. On a weekend the main lanes are busy and the restaurants rush; a weekday is calmer and the shopkeepers talk. The 2026 (29th) festival dates had not been published by the municipality as of early September — check beypazari.bel.tr before planning a group around it; the 2025 edition ran 26–28 September — ⚠ VERIFY the dates and whether you actually want the crowd before bringing a group that weekend. This is our favourite first road day out of Ankara: cheap, easy, and everyone eats too much.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The old quarter lanes and the konak museums — the Yaşayan Müze ('living museum') if you want the interiors.
Hıdırlık Tepesi for the view over the town.
Güveç for lunch, and the 80-katlı baklava afterwards.
Beypazarı kurusu and a crate of the local maden suyu to take home.
The Saturday market in the square, if you land on one.

title: Kızılcahamam: the thermal town and Soğuksu forest
tagline: Hot mineral water and a black-pine national park an hour north — Ankara's answer to a cold weekend.
time: a full day, or a night
when: autumn for the forest colours, winter for the hot water
why: Eighty kilometres north on the Istanbul road, Kızılcahamam is a small town built on hot springs — 'red hamam' in the name — and it has been Ankara's spa since the republic's early days. The town is ringed by thermal hotels with indoor and outdoor pools of genuinely hot mineral water, and most of them sell day-use entry, which is what Ankara does on a grey Sunday in January. Behind the town is Soğuksu National Park, declared in 1959 as one of Turkey's first, a thousand hectares of black pine and fir with marked trails, picnic clearings and a colony of black vultures — real forest, in a province that mostly isn't. Between them they cover both things a steppe capital lacks: hot water and trees.
take: The version we recommend is a Saturday drive up, a long forest walk in Soğuksu in the morning (entry is a small park fee), lunch in the town, and two hours in a thermal pool before driving back — or stay the night if a group wants to make a weekend of it. In autumn the forest is the reason; from December it's the water, with steam over the outdoor pools and snow on the pines. Bring your own towel and flip-flops. ⚠ VERIFY day-use hours and prices at whichever hotel you pick — they change season to season and are written for overnight guests — and check the park is open in deep winter. Buses from AŞTİ run all day; a shared car is easier with four.

title: A night at CSO Ada, the Opera or a state theatre
tagline: The Presidential Symphony, the State Opera and Ballet and the State Theatres all live here — world-class programmes at prices that would be a joke in Istanbul.
when: season runs September to June; book the day tickets go on sale
why: This is Ankara's real edge over every other Turkish city. The Presidential Symphony Orchestra (CSO) — descended from the Ottoman court band, the oldest orchestra in the country — plays in CSO Ada, a 2020 concert campus on Talatpaşa Bulvarı with a 2,000-seat hall of serious acoustic quality. The State Opera and Ballet's home is the pink Opera Sahnesi in Ulus, restored in 2018 to its 1948 look; the State Theatres run more stages here than anywhere else in Turkey; and out at Bilkent the university's own symphony plays a full season. The 2026–27 CSO Ada season, announced on 27 August, runs September to June and brings the Royal Philharmonic with Elisabeth Leonskaja alongside the state opera, choirs and folk ensembles. Because these are state institutions, tickets cost less than a Bestekar bar tab. Ankara does culture because it has an audience of civil servants, academics and diplomats who expect it.
take: Make a Smileys ritual of it: one concert or opera a month, a group of six to ten, a drink on Bestekar or in Ulus afterwards. It's the outing that most surprises newcomers and the one where the conversation afterwards is best. Book early — the good CSO nights sell out in days and the state-subsidised prices are the reason. Dress is smart-casual; the audience is not stuffy. Programmes and ticketing live on the institutions' own sites (cso.gov.tr, operabale.gov.tr, devtiyatro.gov.tr) and the state ticketing platform — ⚠ VERIFY the venue on your ticket, since the state opera performs both at CSO Ada and at its own Ulus house in the same season. If you only do one thing on this list in winter, do this.

sections.title: How to do it
items: CSO Ada Ankara, Talatpaşa Bulvarı — the symphony's home; two halls, a café and a bookshop.
Opera Sahnesi, Ulus — the State Opera and Ballet's historic house.
Devlet Tiyatroları — several central stages; plays in Turkish, but the productions carry.
Bilkent Symphony Orchestra — a full season out at the campus concert hall.
Tickets sell fast and cheap; go on the day of release and buy for the whole group.

title: Ankara döner, Ankara tava and the capital's table
tagline: A döner that isn't the döner you know, lamb baked on orzo, a simit that isn't Istanbul's — the small, stubborn cuisine of a city people say has none.
when: lunchtime — döner is a midday food here and the good shops sell out
why: Ankara gets called a city without a cuisine, usually by people from cities with a sea. It isn't true, it's just that the food is plain and proud. Ankara döner is the clearest case: lamb, never mince, marinated lightly and cooked slowly over oak charcoal, then shaved off the spit in thin leaves and served on pide with nothing but the meat's own fat — no sauce, no salad, and the old Ulus shops will look at you if you ask. Ankara tava is the Sunday dish: lamb braised on orzo (arpa şehriye) in a big tray until the top crisps. Around them are the steppe things — tandır lamb, the Ankara simit (darker and crisper-crusted than Istanbul's), Beypazarı kurusu with tea, Kızılcahamam's mineral water, çubuk pickles from the town of Çubuk, and the honey and dried fruit that come down from the villages to the markets. It is a shepherd's and a civil servant's table: filling, cheap, unshowy.
take: Do döner first, in Ulus, at lunch, at one of the old counters rather than a chain — the room will be plain, the portion will be honest, and you'll understand the dish. Then find Ankara tava on a menu that says 'yöresel' and order it for the table. Work through the rest over a month at the Sunday markets. Prices here are the lowest of any big Turkish city; a good lunch is a Smileys outing that costs nothing to organise. We deliberately name no shops — Ankara's food arguments are as old as the republic and every member has a different 'the real one'. Ask on the group and go with whoever is loudest.

sections.title: The capital's table
items: Ankara döner — lamb, oak-charcoal, sliced in thin leaves, no sauce. Lunch only. Lunch only.
Ankara tava — lamb baked on orzo; a shared dish for a group.
Ankara simidi — darker and crisper-crusted than Istanbul's softer one; buy it from a cart at breakfast.
Beypazarı kurusu and 80-katlı baklava — the tea-time sweets.
Çubuk turşusu — the pickles of Çubuk district, sold in jars at every market.

title: Winter in Ankara: snow in the city, sledges on Elmadağ
tagline: A real winter — dry cold, blue skies, snow on the citadel — and a hill twenty-five kilometres out where the city goes to slide.
when: the morning after a snowfall, December to February
why: Ankara sits at nearly a thousand metres on the Anatolian plateau, and its winter is the real thing: nights well below zero, weeks of dry cold under hard blue skies, and several proper snowfalls a season that turn the citadel and the pines of Kuğulu Park into a postcard. It is the season the city is built for — the concert halls are full, the hamams are full, and salep and roasted chestnuts appear on every corner. For snow you can play in, there is Elmadağ, the mountain some twenty kilometres south-east that gives the city its skyline: a small public ski area on its slopes at around 1,800 metres, free to enter, with sledge and ski hire from the huts when the snow is deep. Ankara treats it as a Sunday sledging hill more than a resort, and that's the honest description.
take: The first snow morning, go up to the citadel walls before it gets trampled — the view over a white city with the steppe hills behind is the one photo of Ankara that changes people's minds. Then Kuğulu Park, a salep, and a concert or a hamam in the evening. Elmadağ is a good group outing on the right day: shared car, real boots, a sledge, tea from the huts, back in the city by dark. Go with expectations set low: there is no snowmaking, the season depends entirely on snowfall, roads and facilities have been poorly kept for years, and the chairlift was reported broken in 2022 with no reliable word since — ⚠ VERIFY that lifts are running before promising anyone skiing rather than sledging. For real skiing, people drive on to Kartalkaya or Ilgaz. For a snowy afternoon with friends, Elmadağ is enough.

title: Atatürk Orman Çiftliği: Gazi's farm
tagline: The model farm Atatürk founded on bare steppe in 1925 — a replica of his Salonica house, the old brewery, and now a huge new nature park on the same land.
when: a weekend morning; the museums open only from 13:00 on the first day of a religious bayram
why: In May 1925 Atatürk bought a stretch of marsh and steppe west of the new capital and set out to prove the land could be farmed. AOÇ — Gazi Orman Çiftliği — became a model farm, a factory complex and Ankara's first public leisure ground in one: dairy, winery, and from 1937 a brewery designed by Ernst Egli, with a Bira Parkı beside it where families drank the farm's own beer under the trees, Atatürk among them. Much of the land has since been carved up — the road, the stadium, the presidential complex — but what remains is a rare open space in the west of the city: the Atatürk Evi, a replica of his birthplace in Salonica; a museum and exhibition hall; a picnic park with old plane trees; and, since September 2025, the metropolitan municipality's Atatürk Çocukları nature park and zoo on 940,000 square metres of the farm's former zoo land.
take: Come on a weekend morning for a slow walk under the trees, the Atatürk house (small, quiet, worth twenty minutes), and a picnic — it is the farm's original purpose and the city still uses it that way. The new nature park is the reason to bring anyone with children. The beer garden is the sad part: the brewery closed decades ago, and as of this writing the farm's own site lists no beer park or bar among its visitable places, so treat the 'beer garden' as history rather than a plan — ⚠ VERIFY whether any restaurant on the farm still serves the old Ankara beer before you promise a group a pint under Gazi's trees. Bring your own picnic; that part is certain.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: Atatürk Evi — a 1981 replica of the Salonica house, furnished in period style, with his personal effects in the museum room upstairs.
The AOÇ museum and exhibition hall — the farm's story, and the early republic's.
The 1930s brewery buildings from outside — Egli's modernist ensemble.
The Atatürk Çocukları nature park and zoo, opened 6 September 2025.
The plant sales greenhouse — Ankara's balcony gardens start here.
